summary: The design crosses four parser architectures with inconsistent dict semantics and currently diverges from qsurl’s case-insensitive vocabulary. The highest risks are operator/name collisions with JSON extraction, first-vs-last operator handling, validation being bypassed or swallowed, and LIKE/regex escaping differences across dialects.

suggestions.title: Resolve case sensitivity before adding aliases
suggestions.rationale: qsurl maps bare startswith, contains, and endswith to ILIKE patterns, while the proposed table assigns those names to case-sensitive LIKE and reserves i* for case-insensitive behavior. That would make the same vocabulary mean different things depending on whether it came from qsurl or direct where_cond input. Choose one contract, then update the translator and compatibility tests together.

suggestions.title: Define an explicit JSON-dict collision policy
suggestions.rationale: PostgreSQL currently treats a dict with no recognized operator as implicit JSONB containment, while BigQuery treats any non-comparison dict key as JSON_VALUE extraction. Reserving contains, regex, like, and related names therefore changes existing inputs such as meta: {contains: x}; this cannot be disambiguated by operand type alone when the operand is a string. Either reserve/document these keys across dialects, introduce an operator namespace, or preserve JSON-key access through a separate form.

suggestions.title: Enforce single-key partial-match dictionaries
suggestions.rationale: AbstractParser._where_element keeps the last dict item, whereas the PostgreSQL Rust builder and generic Rust/BigQuery builders read the first item. The accepted scope says partial operators are single-key, but does not enforce that contract. Reject multi-key dictionaries only when they contain a partial operator, while retaining the intentional multi-operator JSONB behavior.

suggestions.title: Do not rely solely on _where_element for validation
suggestions.rationale: The PostgreSQL dispatcher catches every Rust exception and falls back to Cython, so builder-level validation errors would be swallowed. Direct calls to filter_conditions or the Cython/Rust functions also bypass _where_element. Put validation in a reusable non-rendering validator, invoke it before dispatch and from the normal _where_element lifecycle, and distinguish validation errors from ordinary Rust fallback errors.

suggestions.title: Make escaping ownership explicit per operator
suggestions.rationale: qsurl already emits escaped ILIKE patterns, while the proposed direct startswith/contains/endswith operators need to escape wildcards before adding wildcards. Reusing the same builder branch without distinguishing already-rendered patterns can double-escape qsurl input. Define whether each operator receives a raw value or a ready pattern, and test %, _, backslash, quotes, and pre-quoted values on both paths.

suggestions.title: Replace generic SQL escape assumptions with dialect capabilities
suggestions.rationale: SQLParser has no dialect or escape-character capability, yet the proposal depends on different LIKE escape defaults and LOWER-based case folding. SQL Server, BigQuery, and the generic parser have separate rendering paths, and SQL Server currently has no dict branch at all. Model pattern rendering as a dialect-specific capability or stage the feature per dialect instead of treating generic SQL as one behavior.

suggestions.title: Avoid leaking SQL Server dict support into shared non-SQL parsers
suggestions.rationale: mssql_parser, soql_parser, and cql_parser all consume filter_common’s FilterValue, extract_entries, and process_entry. Adding a Dict variant there requires every shared match and consumer to define behavior, potentially changing SOQL/CQL semantics. Prefer a dialect-specific dict representation or make the shared layer explicitly reject dicts while SQL Server handles them separately.

suggestions.title: Reuse the existing regex safety policy
suggestions.rationale: The existing qsurl residual path caps patterns at 200 characters and rejects nested quantifiers, but parser-level PostgreSQL regex operators would bypass that protection. A length-only guard still admits short pathological patterns. Extract a shared validation policy with a Rust twin, or explicitly document why database-side regex has a different safety boundary, and test both overlong and nested-quantifier cases.

suggestions.title: Build a full dialect/path conformance matrix
suggestions.rationale: Current coverage is strongest for PostgreSQL ILIKE, with a stale-extension probe and direct Rust/Cython comparisons, but the proposed feature adds many operators across eight implementation paths. Add parametrized expected SQL/error cases for every operator, operand type, wildcard escape, JSON collision, multi-key input, and regex guard; include build_query/set_where coverage and explicitly stage the source-tree extension as Makefile requires.
